lines.say: Before dawn on April twenty-eighth, 1908, a farmhouse burned to the ground just north of La Porte, Indiana.
lines.tts: Before dawn on April twenty-eighth, nineteen oh eight, a farmhouse burned to the ground just north of La Porte, Indiana.

lines.say: In the cellar, searchers found the bodies of three children, and a woman. Her head was missing.
Everyone believed the woman was their mother. A widow named Belle Gunness.
Then the digging began.
Behind the house, in a buried garbage pit, they found a farmer who had come all the way from South Dakota to marry her.
Then they found more.
For years, men had been answering a lonely widow's ads in the newspapers. Many of them were never seen again.
This is the story of Belle Gunness, and of the question La Porte has never been able to answer.
She was born Brynhild Paulsdatter Størset, on November eleventh, 1859, in Selbu, a farming district in the hills of central Norway.
lines.tts: She was born Brynhild Paulsdatter Størset, on November eleventh, eighteen fifty-nine, in Selbu, a farming district in the hills of central Norway.

lines.say: She was the youngest of eight children. Her father was a cottar, a tenant who worked another family's land, and a stonecutter.
As a teenager she herded cattle and milked cows on the neighbors' farms, and saved for one thing: a ticket to America.
In Selbu, a story is still told about her: that as a young woman she was attacked at a dance, lost the baby she was carrying, and was never the same. There's no record that it happened.
In 1881, at twenty-one, she crossed the Atlantic to join her older sister in Chicago.
lines.tts: In eighteen eighty-one, at twenty-one, she crossed the Atlantic to join her older sister in Chicago.

lines.say: In America, Brynhild became Bella. Then Belle.
Chicago in the 1880s was one of the fastest-growing cities in the world, and home to more Norwegians than any other city in America.
lines.tts: Chicago in the eighteen eighties was one of the fastest-growing cities in the world, and home to more Norwegians than any other city in America.

lines.say: Belle worked as a servant. In 1884 she married a fellow Norwegian, Mads Sorenson.
lines.tts: Belle worked as a servant. In eighteen eighty-four she married a fellow Norwegian, Mads Sorenson.

lines.say: They opened a candy store. It caught fire. The insurance paid.
Over the years, the candy store and two of their homes burned. Each time, Belle collected.
Two children in the Sorensons' care, Caroline and Axel, died as babies. Doctors blamed an inflammation of the bowel, which can also be a sign of poison. Both children were insured.
Belle and Mads also raised two girls, Myrtle and Lucy, and a foster daughter, Jennie Olson.
On July thirtieth, 1900, Mads came home with a headache. Belle said she gave him a powder for it. Then he died.
lines.tts: On July thirtieth, nineteen hundred, Mads came home with a headache. Belle said she gave him a powder for it. Then he died.

lines.say: It was the one day on which two of his life insurance policies overlapped: the old one ending, and a new, bigger one beginning.
One doctor suspected poison. Another blamed his heart. There was no autopsy, and no charges.
Belle collected on both policies: by most accounts, eight thousand five hundred dollars.
She used it to buy a farm, about sixty miles to the east, outside La Porte, Indiana.
In November 1901, Belle moved to La Porte with Jennie, Myrtle and Lucy.
lines.tts: In November nineteen oh one, Belle moved to La Porte with Jennie, Myrtle and Lucy.

lines.say: The farm sat at the north edge of town, on McClung Road: more than forty acres, a big brick house, a barn, and an orchard.
La Porte was a busy factory town. Belle kept to herself, and she worked hard.
Within months, she married again. On April first, 1902, at the First Baptist Church in La Porte, she wed Peter Gunness, a Norwegian widower who had once boarded with her family in Chicago.
lines.tts: Within months, she married again. On April first, nineteen oh two, at the First Baptist Church in La Porte, she wed Peter Gunness, a Norwegian widower who had once boarded with her family in Chicago.

lines.say: Peter brought his two little daughters. Within about a week, the baby died, while she was alone with Belle. No one ever determined why.
On December sixteenth, 1902, Peter died too.
lines.tts: On December sixteenth, nineteen oh two, Peter died too.

lines.say: Belle said a heavy sausage grinder had fallen from a high shelf and struck him on the head.
The coroner weighed the grinder, and measured how far it could have fallen.
He was suspicious. But in the end, there were no charges. Belle collected about three thousand dollars in life insurance.
Peter's brother came and took his surviving daughter, Swanhild, away with him.
In 1903, Belle had a son. She named him Philip.
lines.tts: In nineteen oh three, Belle had a son. She named him Philip.

lines.say: Hired men came to work on the farm. Some stayed. Some, people noticed, simply left, sometimes without their things.
In 1906, Jennie Olson, the foster daughter Belle had raised since she was a baby, disappeared.
lines.tts: In nineteen oh six, Jennie Olson, the foster daughter Belle had raised since she was a baby, disappeared.

lines.say: Belle said Jennie had gone away to school, in Los Angeles by most accounts. Nobody ever saw her again.
By then, Belle was writing letters. A lot of them. Her mail carrier said she sent eight to ten a day.
She was placing ads in the marriage columns of newspapers, many of them Norwegian-language papers read by farmers all over the Midwest.

One of them, as a newspaper reprinted it in 1908, read: Comely widow, who owns large farm in one of the finest districts in La Porte county, Indiana, desires to make the acquaintance of gentleman equally well provided, with view of joining fortunes. No replies by letter considered unless sender is willing to follow answer with personal visit.
lines.tts: One of them, as a newspaper reprinted it in nineteen oh eight, read: Comely widow, who owns large farm in one of the finest districts in La Porte county, Indiana, desires to make the acquaintance of gentleman equally well provided, with view of joining fortunes. No replies by letter considered unless sender is willing to follow answer with personal visit.

lines.say: Men answered. Farmers and laborers, most of them Norwegian immigrants like her, many of them with savings.
She told them what to do. Sell everything. Bring cash. Sew the money into your clothes. Tell no one.
John Moe came from Elbow Lake, Minnesota, with more than a thousand dollars. Within about a week, he was gone.
Henry Gurholdt came from Scandinavia, Wisconsin, with about fifteen hundred. Belle said he'd gone off to Chicago with some horse traders. She kept his trunk, and his fur coat.
Ole Budsberg, a widower from Iola, Wisconsin, was last seen in April 1907 at the La Porte Savings Bank, where he had turned a mortgage on his land into cash.
lines.tts: Ole Budsberg, a widower from Iola, Wisconsin, was last seen in April nineteen oh seven at the La Porte Savings Bank, where he had turned a mortgage on his land into cash.

lines.say: When his sons wrote to ask where he was, Belle answered that he had never arrived.
In 1906, a bachelor farmer from near Aberdeen, South Dakota, answered one of Belle's ads. His name was Andrew Helgelien.
lines.tts: In nineteen oh six, a bachelor farmer from near Aberdeen, South Dakota, answered one of Belle's ads. His name was Andrew Helgelien.

lines.say: For sixteen months, they wrote to each other.
In one letter, she told him how to carry his money, sewn inside his underwear, and wrote: Do not say one word about it to anyone, not even your nearest relative.
In another, she wrote: I do not think you will leave me after you have first come here. That I am sure of.
In early January 1908, Andrew came to La Porte. He told his brother he'd be home in a week.
lines.tts: In early January nineteen oh eight, Andrew came to La Porte. He told his brother he'd be home in a week.

lines.say: He had his savings, nearly three thousand dollars, sent to a bank in La Porte. Belle took the money in cash.
The next day, Andrew was gone.
Someone else was watching: Belle's hired man, Ray Lamphere. By most accounts he was in love with her, and jealous of Andrew.
In February 1908, Belle fired him. Then she went after him: she had him arrested for trespassing, tried to get a peace bond against him, and asked to have him declared insane.
lines.tts: In February nineteen oh eight, Belle fired him. Then she went after him: she had him arrested for trespassing, tried to get a peace bond against him, and asked to have him declared insane.

lines.say: Back in South Dakota, Andrew's brother, Asle, kept writing, asking where Andrew had gone.
Belle wrote back that Andrew had gone away, perhaps to Norway, and suggested Asle sell his brother's stock and come help her look.
She was still writing to other men. On March first, 1908, she told a man in Kansas City that she was a lonely Norwegian woman, and asked whether he could put up a thousand dollars in cash.
lines.tts: She was still writing to other men. On March first, nineteen oh eight, she told a man in Kansas City that she was a lonely Norwegian woman, and asked whether he could put up a thousand dollars in cash.

lines.say: On April twenty-seventh, 1908, Belle went to a La Porte lawyer, Melvin Leliter, and made her will, leaving everything to her children.
lines.tts: On April twenty-seventh, nineteen oh eight, Belle went to a La Porte lawyer, Melvin Leliter, and made her will, leaving everything to her children.

lines.say: She told him she was afraid Ray Lamphere was going to kill her, and burn down her house.
That evening, by one account, she bought cakes, a toy train, and two gallons of kerosene.
Around four o'clock the next morning, the new hired man, Joe Maxson, woke to the smell of smoke.
He shouted for Belle and the children. No one answered. He ran for help.
By the time the fire was out, the big brick house had collapsed into its own cellar.
In the ruins, searchers found four bodies: Myrtle, eleven. Lucy, nine. Philip, five. And a woman, without a head.
That same day, the sheriff went looking for Ray Lamphere. By evening, according to the newspapers, he was under arrest, charged with murdering Belle Gunness and her children.
Lamphere said he had only seen the fire as he passed by on his way to work.
The first newspaper stories called it a tragedy: a widow and her children, burned in their beds.
That story lasted one week.
In early May, a stranger walked into the sheriff's office. It was Asle Helgelien, from South Dakota, with a stack of Belle's letters to his brother.
He didn't believe Andrew had simply left.
Joe Maxson remembered something. In March, Belle had him fill and level a pit of garbage near the hog lot.
On May fifth, 1908, they dug there.
lines.tts: On May fifth, nineteen oh eight, they dug there.

lines.say: Wrapped in sacks, they found the remains of Andrew Helgelien.
Two feet below him lay Jennie Olson, the foster daughter who had supposedly gone away to school.
They kept digging. By the next night, nine bodies had come out of the yard.
Most had been cut apart. Some were men. Some were children.
Searchers recovered the remains of at least a dozen people from the farm. Only a few were ever named: Andrew Helgelien. Jennie Olson. Ole Budsberg. John Moe, and possibly Henry Gurholdt.
The rest were never named. Seven of them were buried in La Porte's potter's field.
Estimates of how many people Belle Gunness killed run from fourteen to more than forty.
And the whole country was watching La Porte.
On Sunday, May tenth, thousands of people came out to the farm. The railroads and trolleys alone brought about four thousand more into town.
Peddlers at the gate sold lemonade and lunches, and souvenir pictures. The best seller was a photograph of Belle and her three children.
But was the woman in the cellar really Belle?
Her head was never found.
Neighbors, and at least one local doctor who knew her, said the body was far too small to be hers. Other doctors said the fire could explain it. No reliable measurement survives.
A Chicago chemist later reported finding poison in the stomachs of the woman and two of the children.
The sheriff and a miner named Louis Schultz washed the ashes through a sluice, like gold.
On May nineteenth, they found two dental plates with false teeth. Belle's dentist said they were hers.
The sheriff said it proved, beyond the shadow of a doubt, that Belle had died in the fire. The coroner agreed.
Not everyone did. The teeth had come through a fire that destroyed a house, and they were in good shape. Many people believed they had been planted.
Three days later, a grand jury indicted Ray Lamphere for arson and murder. It also indicted Belle Gunness, for the murder of Andrew Helgelien, though the coroner had just declared her dead.
Ray Lamphere went on trial in November 1908, at the La Porte County Courthouse.
lines.tts: Ray Lamphere went on trial in November nineteen oh eight, at the La Porte County Courthouse.

lines.say: Choosing a jury was hard. Several men were excused because they believed Belle Gunness was still alive.
Lamphere's lawyer, Wirt Worden, argued that she was.
Witnesses testified that they had seen Belle, alive, that summer.
On Thanksgiving Day, November twenty-sixth, the jury gave its verdict: not guilty of murder. Guilty of arson.
He was sentenced to two to twenty-one years in the state prison at Michigan City.
He served about a year. On December thirtieth, 1909, Ray Lamphere died of tuberculosis.
lines.tts: He served about a year. On December thirtieth, nineteen oh nine, Ray Lamphere died of tuberculosis.

lines.say: After his death, newspapers printed what they called his confession. In it, he said he had set the fire, and that the body in the cellar was Belle.
Other men told other stories. That Lamphere had helped her escape. That the woman in the cellar was a housekeeper lured from Chicago. That Belle had killed forty-two men.
Those stories came secondhand, after Lamphere was dead, and they contradict each other.
Within days of the fire, people started seeing Belle Gunness.
In Syracuse. In Tacoma. For more than twenty years, letters reached La Porte from all over the country.
In 1931, in Los Angeles, a woman named Esther Carlson was charged with poisoning an eighty-one-year-old man, August Lindstrom, for two thousand dollars.
lines.tts: In nineteen thirty-one, in Los Angeles, a woman named Esther Carlson was charged with poisoning an eighty-one-year-old man, August Lindstrom, for two thousand dollars.

lines.say: She died of tuberculosis before her trial.
Two people who had once lived in La Porte looked at her body and said it was Belle. In her trunk were photographs of three children.
Esther Carlson had always denied it. Nothing ever proved it.
In 2007, a team from the University of Indianapolis set out to answer the question with science.
lines.tts: In two thousand seven, a team from the University of Indianapolis set out to answer the question with science.

lines.say: It was led by Andrea Simmons, a graduate student, a lawyer, and a La Porte native, with forensic anthropologist Stephen Nawrocki.
On November fifth, 2007, they opened the grave at Forest Home Cemetery near Chicago, where the headless woman was buried beside Mads Sorenson.
lines.tts: On November fifth, two thousand seven, they opened the grave at Forest Home Cemetery near Chicago, where the headless woman was buried beside Mads Sorenson.

lines.say: Inside the casket, with the woman's bones, they found the remains of two children no one had expected.
They hoped to match DNA from the bones with saliva on envelopes Belle had licked a century before.
But the samples were too old and too degraded. The tests were inconclusive.
The house on McClung Road is long gone, and the land is private property.
Belle's story is kept at the La Porte County Historical Society Museum, on Indiana Avenue.
In 2008, a hundred years after the fire, descendants of her victims came to La Porte to put headstones on graves that had been unmarked since 1908.
lines.tts: In two thousand eight, a hundred years after the fire, descendants of her victims came to La Porte to put headstones on graves that had been unmarked since nineteen oh eight.

lines.say: Andrew Helgelien lies in Patton Cemetery. His stone calls him the last victim.
Most of the others were never named.
Whether Belle Gunness died in that fire, or walked away into the dark and lived out her life under another name, no one has ever proved.
More than a hundred years later, La Porte is still asking.
